newsitem.title: USA: Facing death in six days, prisoner still has hope.
newsitem.headline: Facing death in six days, prisoner still has hope.

text.p: Facing execution in six days, convicted murderer Coleman Wayne Gray says he tries not to think about dying and still has faith in "the best judicial system in the world".
Gray, 39, is scheduled to die by lethal injection next Wednesday in Virginia for the May 1985 murder of grocery store manager Richard McClelland.
In a telephone interview with Reuters from his prison cell on death row Thursday, Gray insisted he was not the murderer but was the victim of false testimony.

"I believe we have the best judicial system in the world but sometimes mistakes are made and mistakes were made here. Now that it's been shown that false testimony was given, I hope the system will do the right thing," he said in the interview, during which he was both calm and articulate.

Gray was convicted largely on the testimony of co-defendant Melvin Tucker of robbing and abducting McClelland and shooting him six times in the back of the head, despite his pleas for mercy. Gray says Tucker was the trigger man.

At the penalty stage of the trial, Tucker testified that Gray bragged of committing two other murders as well -- the 1984 killings of Lisa Sorrell and her three-year-old daughter Shanta, in much the same way he murdered McClelland.

In an affadavit filed this week to the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Tucker recanted that testimony, saying he was forced to perjure himself by the prosecution to avoid the death penalty himself. But Tucker still maintains that Gray killed McClelland.

"The story I gave about Gray looking in the newspaper and referring to a picture of the Sorrells was a lie. My testimony concerning Coleman Gray telling me that he killed the Sorrell woman and child was a lie," Tucker said in his affidavit.

The Commonwealth of Virginia said in response that the defence had not raised any new arguments. "Such a recantation of penalty-stage testimony is incapable of constituting 'clear and convincing evidence' that Gray is not guilty of capital murder," the state said.

The court is expected to rule within the next two days on Gray's request for a stay of execution. If it rejects his petition, Gray will be left with only two legal recourses -- an appeal to the Surpreme Court, which has already rejected his appeal once, and a bid for clemency to Virginia Gov. George Allen.
What does it feel like to know you may die in six days?
Gray said he tried to deal with it as best he could by keeping busy, reading and praying.

"I'm sleeping nights, not soundly but some," he said. "I try not to think about dying but sometimes it's hard. Nobody wants to think about dying. I just put it in the hands of the Lord. I can only hope and continue to pray things will work out for me."
Gray has been here once before. In December 1995, his execution was stayed a day before he was scheduled to die. This time, he said, he felt better prepared.

He said he thought about McClelland and his family often. "I hope they can find it in their hearts to forgive me for my involvement. I realise my participation in the crime was wrong but I did not take McClelland's life."
McClelland was 49 at the time of his death. He left a sick wife, who has since died, and four children.
"He was a good husband and a good father and a wonderful boss, the best I ever had," said Nita Hengel, who worked with McClelland at the grocery store.
Gray said he believed in heaven and hell and hoped his spirit would go to heaven and "reside with Jesus."
He said he was convinced the state of Virginia was determined to put him to death rather than face up to questions about the way his case was handled.
"They would rather see me dead than have these injustices exposed. I still hope they will do the right thing," he said.
